source.title: MassAlloc Attention: Let Attention Allocate Its Own Compute
source.authors: Jing-Ze Shi; Zhang-Yang Peng; Xian-Duo Li; Yan-Lin Qi; Xiao-Tian Lin; Hao-Xian Chen; Liang-Dong Wang; Guang Liu; Yu-Yu Luo

record.tranche_reason: It measures perplexity against total training FLOPs across model scales for MALA and FullAttn, bearing on the loss-versus-compute relationship, but does not fit or test the original power-law model.
record.gate_note: The scaling-law experiment reports perplexity curves over five model sizes and two training stages. It does not report fitted exponents or per-size perplexity values in text or tables. Downstream benchmark scores are not linked to pretraining loss or used to test predictability; matched-work and latency results do not test the stated scaling-law claims.
record.test_reason: The 'scaling laws' experiment uses the scaling-law framing to compare its own attention method (MALA) with FullAttn, MoBA and DSA. It plots perplexity against FLOPs for five sizes (0.6B–14B), shown only as a figure. It fits no power law, reports no exponents or per-size values, and makes no extrapolation, allocation search or shape study. The only stated results are MALA-vs-FullAttn gaps at 14B (<0.001 perplexity, 2.5%/23.1% fewer FLOPs), which measure the method's efficiency, not whether loss follows a power law. Training follows 'compute-optimal scaling principles' as a recipe, which is assumed, not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct: the authors conclude that MALA tracks FullAttn perplexity across 0.6B–14B with fewer training FLOPs, a larger saving at 32K, and comparable downstream scores at 14B and 32B.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses normalized-mass attention allocation and reports perplexity-versus-FLOPs scaling curves; it does not reproduce the original scaling-law fitting procedure or compute-optimal allocation analysis.

fits_no_version.finding: Across 0.6B–14B, a sparse post-score attention variant (MALA) tracks FullAttn perplexity versus total training FLOPs, shifting the curve to lower FLOPs (2.5% at 4K, 23.1% at 32K, 14B).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Efficient attention variants can preserve the dense loss-versus-compute scaling curve while reducing compute.

record.code_released: Open-sourced at flash-sparse-attention; URL not stated.
record.problems: Perplexity values are shown only in a plot and no fitted exponents or power-law goodness-of-fit are reported. Parameter count, token count, and compute are not independently varied in the reported scaling sweep.
record.rows_left_out: Downstream benchmark scores are not rows because they are not related to pretraining loss or tested for predictability from scale; other allocation and latency results do not measure the claim versions.

untested.parts: No power-law fit or exponent; only five sizes (~1.5 orders of compute) shown in a figure; parameters and tokens scaled together.
No small-run fit used to predict larger runs.
Uses compute-optimal token budgets as a recipe and does not search for the optimum.
Downstream scores are reported only at 14B/32B and are not related to scale or loss.

record.verdict_notes: This is a method paper. 'Scaling laws' names an experiment design, not a test of the claim. The rows should be relinked to none, and the reader's 'tests'/T2 should become uses_without_test/T4.

versions.untested_parts: The paper reports perplexity against total training FLOPs, but does not fit a power law, report exponents, establish a several-orders-of-magnitude power-law form, or isolate parameter-count and token-count effects from compute.
No fitting on small runs followed by prediction of much larger runs is reported.
No search for a loss-minimising parameter/token allocation at fixed compute is reported.
The study does not isolate depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count to measure their effect on loss.
No other modality or training-regime power-law test is reported.
Downstream scores are reported, but the study does not test whether they are predictable from scale or pretraining loss.
The study does not compare fitting choices or demonstrate disagreement between fitted laws or curvature away from a power law.
